uses: Garlic turns up in old Egyptian, Greek and Indian medical texts, offered for headaches, sore throats, chest complaints and stomach troubles. In folk practice the bulb was eaten or made into syrups with honey or vinegar for coughs and colds, and it was a main ingredient in the Four Thieves vinegar said to guard against plague. Culpeper called it the poor man's treacle, meaning a cheap remedy for nearly everything. Garlic is also traditionally taken to help keep the heart and blood vessels in good order.
energetics: Culpeper called garlic hot and dry in the fourth degree, the strongest heat
caution_pregnancy: Garlic by mouth in more than food amounts may not be safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding; the EMA does not recommend medicinal garlic then. Little is known about putting garlic on the skin while pregnant or nursing. Normal cooking amounts aren't the concern.
caution_medications: Garlic supplements may increase bleeding, so take care with blood thinners (anticoagulants) and anti-platelet drugs, including aspirin. Do not combine garlic supplements with the HIV medicines saquinavir and ritonavir: garlic can lower the drug level and lead to treatment failure or drug resistance. Tell your doctors and pharmacist if you take garlic supplements.
caution_conditions: Stop garlic supplements a week before surgery because of the bleeding risk. Side effects include bad breath and body odor, belly pain, bloating, gas, nausea, headache, dizziness, heavy sweating and bleeding. Allergic reactions, sometimes severe, can include skin rashes, sore eyes, a runny nose or tight airways. Medicinal use isn't established for children under 12.
caution_duration: Garlic by mouth has been used safely in studies lasting up to 7 years. If you take it for a cold, see a practitioner if symptoms last more than a week.
caution_topical: Fresh raw garlic on the skin can cause severe irritation and even chemical burns; don't bind it to the skin. Some prepared topical forms appear safe. Contact dermatitis has been reported.
garden_harvest_timing: Plant cloves in fall; dig the following summer when about half the leaves have turned brown, then cure the bulbs in an airy room for three to four weeks.
garden_water: Shallow-rooted and drought-sensitive while bulbs form; stop watering as the leaves wither
notes: The part used is the bulb, filed here under root. Likes well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Hardneck types send up curly scapes that can be snapped off and eaten. Grieve records that the Greeks left garlic at crossroads for Hecate, and that in the Odyssey a garlic-like herb kept Ulysses from Circe's spell.
